No Child Left Behind (NCLB)

 NCLB performance mandates, embedded within state
 accountability systems, are centrally focused on a school’s
 percentage of students at or above proficient.
 Universal proficiency mandates apply to numerous relevant
 subgroups.
 The result has been renewed attention on achievement gaps
 and strategies for their reduction.
 The mandate to close achievement gaps often avoids critical
 examination. This paper/presentation seeks:
 to ground the discussion of achievement gaps and their
 amelioration within an explicit EEO framework; and
 to put forward a morally compelling and quantifiable criterion
 by which to judge whether achievement based EEO exists.

Equal Educational Opportunity (EEO)

 What is the moral imperative to close achievement gaps? This
 demand is built into NCLB but often goes unquestioned.
 The most obvious ethical foundation upon which to base the
 reduction of achievement gaps is Equal Educational
 Opportunity. That is, the existence of achievement gaps is
 symptomatic of a system lacking EEO.
 Implicit within the gap closing accountability mandates of
 NCLB is a very stringent notion of EEO that bears clarification.

Formalist versus Results Based Conceptions

 Conceptions of EEO can roughly be divided into two groups:
 formalist versus results-based
 A formalist conception of EEO requires only the absence of
 formal barriers to access—for example, de jure segregation.
 Less stringent formalist conceptions call for equalizing various
 inputs (e.g., the quality of teachers, library holdings, etc.)
 Formalist conceptions of EEO are currently out of favor.
 Accountability systems founded on NCLB achievement
 mandates have ushered in an emphasis on outcomes/results.

Results Based Conceptions
 Results-based conceptions of EEO employ educational
 outcomes to ascertain whether EEO exists (e.g., achievement
 test scores, graduation rates, etc.)
 Results based conceptions differ from formal approaches in
 that they take into account the entering characteristics of
 students.
 Results-based conceptions of EEO differ in the extent to
 which equality in outcomes must occur across the types of
 educational results (e.g., what subjects) and within those
 types (to what extent—equal scale scores versus equal
 percentages above a threshold).
 Strict equality of results both across and within types marks
 the most demanding end of the continuum. A view which
 nobody, to our knowledge, endorses.

Conditional versus Unconditional Thresholds

 NCLB exemplifies a relatively strong results-based conception
 of EEO, namely an unconditional threshold conception.
 By 2014, without conditioning upon race, socio-economic
 status, gender, or prior achievement, NCLB requires all
 students perform at or above a state defined proficiency
 threshold in reading, writing, mathematics, and science.
 Though morally compelling, placing sole responsibility on
 schools to fulfill these requirements is guaranteed to fail.
 Our goal is to introduce a more rigorous measure of EEO
 based upon a conditional threshold conception that better
 illustrates (un)equal educational opportunity.
 To avoid impoverishing EEO by looking only at test results, we
 focus on an aspect of EEO manifest in achievement
 data—Equal Educational Opportunity for Achievement (EEOA)

Achievement Gaps and EEOA

 If quantifying EEOA is the goal, how can one approach this task.
 A reasonable criterion is that we have obtained educational
 equity when representatives of different racial, gender, and
 socioeconomic origins have about the same probabilities of
 reaching different educational outcomes [Levin, 1994, p. 168].

 This criterion is probabilistic in nature. We modify Levin’s criterion
 using conditional threshold conception of EEOA.
 EEOA requires that representatives of different racial, gender,
 and socioeconomic subgroups have equal chances of
 reaching any academic proficiency threshold conditional upon
 recent achievement.

Estimation
 Logistic regression is used to estimate the probability of
 reaching the performance threshold.

 exp(b0 + b1 x + b2 g + b3 xg )
 Pr(Y = 1 | X = x , G = g ) =
 1 + exp(b0 + b1 x + b2 g + b3 xg )

 Estimation is problematic because the dependent variable is
 measured with error. That is, the discreet dependent variable is
 subject to misclassification.
 Recent advances in the analysis of additive measurement error
 models allow for the estimation of the model parameters given
 known misclassification probabilities [Küchenhoff et al., 2006,
 Cook and Stefanski, 1994].
 Estimation of model parameters was performed using the R
 software language with the SIMEX
 library [R Development Core Team, 2006].

 Two Criticisms

Not Demanding Enough?

 Two potential criticisms of EEOA are that it is not demanding
 enough while another is that is it too demanding.
 With regard to the former, it appears that EEOA, which
 conditions upon prior achievement, fails to close achievement
 gaps for groups differing at the outset.
 An outcomes based conception of EEO requires “parity among
 groups of individuals on all educational outcomes that affect an
 individual’s chances to enjoy other social goods [Howe, 1989,
 p. 333].
 Equal probability for advanced, however, is not equivalent to
 adding a fixed amount to regular intervals to each group’s
 achievement score (i.e., equal treatment inputs).
 We consider the education system as an ergodic stochastic
 process. As such, EEOA implies that all groups will converge to
 the same steady state.

Too Demanding?

 Even after adjusting for prior achievement, we do not mean to
 suggest that EEOA gaps are the “fault” of bad teachers or
 schools.
 The primary purpose of our analyses is not the uncover the
 “blame worthy perpetrator” [Edley, 2006].
 Lack of resources outside of school continue to diminish a
 students chances for advancement even after adjustment for
 prior achievement.
 However, the gap is something that society in toto is
 responsible for.
 Our goal is to try and put as fine a point as possible on
 achievement disparities and to help “marshal a consensus to
 narrow [them]” [Edley, 2006].
